beats.lead: Sony's own controller lost a core feature for two years over a lawsuit.
beats.text: In February 2002, Immersion Corporation sued Sony, and Microsoft, for patent infringement over the vibration technology in the DualShock controller.
beats.note: Nintendo wasn't named: its Rumble Pak used a separately patented design.

beats.text: Microsoft settled straight away, buying a 10% stake in Immersion. Sony fought the case instead.
beats.note: That decision cost it years in court and tens of millions more than Microsoft ever paid.

beats.text: A jury awarded Immersion $82 million on 21 September 2004; with interest, the total reached $90.7 million.
beats.note: A federal court upheld the verdict in March 2006 and ordered Sony to stop selling the infringing controllers, though the order was stayed during appeal.

beats.text: At E3 2006, Sony announced the new PlayStation 3 controller would ship with no vibration at all.
beats.note: Sony said this avoided interference with the controller's new motion sensor; Immersion's own president was publicly sceptical of that explanation.

beats.context: dollars Sony agreed to pay Immersion in the March 2007 settlement, on top of $30.6 million already paid in licence fees.

beats.line: The PS3 launched silent. Rumble came back in 2008.
